To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

caveolin and flotillin are present in the vesicle structures of P. vivox-infected red blood cells, and that they are involved with the transport and release specific parasite antigens and the uptake of plasma protein.
caveolae and flotilline-2 are present and functional in P. vivax blood stages.

the proteins caveolin-2 and flotillin are present in caveola- vesicle complexes (CVPs) of Plasmodial vivax-infected red blood cells (PvRBCs), and that the expression of caveolin-2 is regulated during the blood cycle of the parasite.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification, characterization and localization of caveolin proteins in P. vivax.
the identification and characterization of caveolins and other caveolae proteins in P. vivax infected erythrocytes.
the role of caveolins and CVC in protein trafficking in the blood stages P. vivax.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CVC are a key component in the parasite protein-trafficking system, which plays a critical role in the survival of the parasite in the host.
caveolins are involved in the protein-traficking pathway that connect P. vivax parasite-encoded proteins with erythrocytes cytoplasm and cell surface throughout the erythrocytic cycle.

the presence of these proteins in the CVC of P.vivax-infected erythocytes suggests their involvement in the protein-traffficking pathway that connects parasite-encoded proteins with erythrocyte surface throughout the asexually cycle of vivax parasite.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of caveolin and flotillin in the P. vivax-infected erythocyte membrane is a novel finding that could be important in the understanding of parasite biology.

caveolae and their associated proteins are present in the P. falciparum- and P. vivax-parasitized red cells, and that these proteins may be involved in parasite survival in vivo and in the development of severe malaria.

the presence of caveolin-2 and -3 and flotillin in CVC of P vivax-infected cells suggests that caveolae are involved in the trafficking of parasite antigens and in the uptake and transcytose of plasma components.
The main takeaway from our work is that
P. vivax infection induces the development of CVC in the membrane of the infected erythrocell.
caveolins are present in the P.  vivax-infected red blood cell, and they may be involved in the transport of parasite proteins from the cytosol to the cell surface.

the presence of caveolin and flotillin proteins in the CVC of P vivax–infected erythroctes suggests that these organelles are involved in the protein-traficking pathway that connects parasite-encoded proteins with erythrocyte cell membrane.
